result.b_biggest_risk: The unit economics rest on unproven inputs. Closing owners may mostly hold consumer-heavy, owner-dependent books that do not hold 70% retention at 0.25-0.4x. The invented 19% contribution on absorbed crews may also fail, as crews are free to leave in a labor-short market. Then no hub reaches the roughly EUR 1.55M break-even or the EUR 3M+ scale that makes a Meister pay, and the business stays a loss-making micro-firm collection that investors will not fund.

decisive_factors: Existence proof: transformer intermediaries (Giga at $150M+ infrastructure sales, Ayr at $500M+ in orders on about $25M raised, plus JCL, Maddox and Sunbelt Solomon) already reach $100M+ revenue on tens of millions of capital. B has no US precedent of a non-national operator that a hospital chose over cash and kept past year 3.

Demand and willingness to pay are better evidenced in A. Lead times are 128-160+ weeks, buyers are documented paying 3-15% for speed, and individual deals are about $2M. B's price only works if a startup with no route density beats the hospital's own cost by 17-24%, and that baseline is unbenchmarked.

A's first stages are cheap and quick to falsify or monetize: dealer quotes plus buyer calls in 14 days, then fee-only brokering with no inventory. B's stand-up and sales cycles are long (hospital CFO and board, 5-year terms, 90-180 day payer enrollment), and its test needs hospital executives to hand over cost data.

B has a documented customer rejection (Kootenai fired the closest analog, PAML) and stacked legal tails: CMS 1833(h)(5)(A) wholly-owned billing, 42 CFR 424.73 and EKRA. B's neutrality claim also conflicts with its own hub and JV upside layers. A's regulatory tails (DPA hoarding, EO 14420 provenance, tariffs) are more manageable.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are weak and both critics left them wounded. Each has a median case near break-even (A about $30M revenue at 11-13% gross margin and a 25-person team; B about $7-8M after correcting its own inconsistent funnel). Each has an upside of roughly $8-12M EBITDA at 2-8% probability. So the choice turns on which is more likely to produce a real, modestly profitable business and which fails faster and cheaper if wrong.

A wins on that. The shortage it addresses is documented, with lead times of 128-160+ weeks and premiums for speed that buyers have actually paid. The deals are large, around $2M each, so a few fee or principal transactions already matter. Direct peers (Giga, Ayr, JCL, Maddox) show the intermediary model scales on modest capital. Even if the date-certain premium collapses, a brokerage or dealer business with real gross profit is a plausible fallback. A's open question is supply access. The two-week test doesn't cover it, but fee-only brokering in months 3-12 does, and it needs no inventory.

B has a worse structure. A hospital's best alternatives are cash from Quest or Labcorp, doing it in-house, or advice from Mayo, ARUP or Chi. Its one real analog failed and the customer left. Cost advantage, neutrality demand and the 33% win rate are all unsupported guesses, and the regulation (Medicare billing, EKRA, state rules) is heavier. Its upside is mostly pass-through revenue, and the hub and JV layers undercut its only moat.

A's chief weakness is that it has no moat. The shortage could also fade in 2027-29, but that risk is known and priced into A's matched-book design.
result.a_biggest_risk: No defensible edge and no proven supply: dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already stock or quote fast units, OEMs have no reason to give a newcomer slots, and the cancelled-unit supply is unevidenced. As new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29 the speed premium could compress to a roughly 5% dealer spread.
result.b_biggest_risk: No stayer health system signs a 5-year open-book contract with a startup instead of taking a national's management offer, using Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice, or keeping the work in-house. The required 17-24% cost advantage is unproven, the one documented customer of this model fired its operator, and the structure carries Medicare billing, EKRA and 42 CFR 424.73 risk.

decisive_factors: Floor vs. ceiling: B buys existing cash-flowing, recurring-revenue businesses, so even a failed thesis leaves an owned operating asset, while A's median case is roughly break-even on $30M of revenue and its premium may not exist.

Failure mode severity: all three of A's critics rated their objections fatal (competition, pricing, capital/execution), and the supply side (assignable cancelled units, OEM slots for a newcomer) is unevidenced and untested. B's critics rated theirs serious, and the main unknown (the price sellers accept) is directly testable.

Time-limited vs. durable demand: A depends on a transformer shortage that Rystad, new OEM capacity in 2027-28, and the plan's own pre-mortem say is easing, so it is structurally a peak-scarcity trade. B rides a multi-year family-succession wave with no expiry.

Capital and expected value: B needs about $10-14M of anchor equity, deal-by-deal, with proof of funds and a kill rule. Its modeled outcomes are 1.5x median and 3.5x at 21% IRR in the upside. A needs about $30M of equity plus a $50-60M warehouse for 7-10% gross margins and a 2-3% unconditional upside.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are weak, and neither would get my money unconditionally. The question is which has the better expected outcome and the less fatal objections.

A, after being rebuilt, is a dealer-financier. The original fleet is withdrawn. Its own refined numbers give a median of $30M revenue at about 11-13% gross margin, roughly $4-5M gross profit, about break-even after a 25-person team. The second-round critic argues the blended margin is nearer 7-10% and the $120M upside is overstated by $10M or more. The upside is about 2-3% likely unconditionally. The 'nobody holds stock' gap was false, so the premium has to survive JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr and FluxCo. Supply depends on OEMs or cancelled-order holders handing slots to a newcomer, and nothing shows that is assignable. The moat is none. The scarcity rent is also fading as new OEM capacity lands in 2027-28.

B is a conventional buy-and-build, but it is a real one. It buys cash-flowing, contract-based businesses, with no timing cliff and a succession wave behind it. Entry at 5.5-6.5x is roughly the going lower-middle-market sponsor price, which makes closing deals plausible. The downside is bounded: an owned laundry at 3.0-3.5x leverage, not a stranded inventory bet. Median returns are mediocre (1.5x, about 8% IRR), but the upside (3.5x, about 21%) has a concrete mechanism in margin synergy and scale multiple expansion. The main risk is price discipline, and the owner-call test measures it directly.

B has a higher floor, a more durable market, less fatal critiques and lower capital needs.
result.a_biggest_risk: The premise that buyers will pay a durable premium for date-certain delivery is probably false or short-lived. Dealers already stock and quote comparable units, OEMs have no reason to give a newcomer slots they can sell directly, and new capacity compresses the spread toward a 5% dealer margin. The business then sits at about break-even with no moat.
result.b_biggest_risk: Family owners may not sell to a new, unproven vehicle at 6.5x or below. Strategics and PE platforms with the same rollover offers set the price at 8x or more. Entry at 7.5x cuts the base-case IRR to about 12.5% and the median to about 4%, so the business then fails or reduces to a generic roll-up with adverse selection.

decisive_factors: Demand evidence: A rides a shortage that is documented in many sources (128 to 160+ week lead times, buyers prepaying, a 3.4% premium paid to save years). B has no evidence that any owner wants a growth cap and would pay for it, and its own pass test selects the cases where the prime loses money.

Time to revenue and capital at risk: A can book fee-only brokered deals within weeks, then take at most $15M of matched-book risk on about $30M of equity. B cannot earn until spring 2028 and first needs a sponsor, a surety line and references, plus $20-25M of retained fixed-price risk.

Payoff shape: A's upside is a $8-12M EBITDA dealer-financier that an acquirer would plausibly buy for $80-150M. B's upside is $4-7M EBITDA, and its median ends as a $20-40M sale to an ISP, with a negative-skew tail (a rotor failure on early package 3 can wipe out capital).

Fatality of the objections: A's biggest holes (existing dealers, OEM slot assignability) are testable cheaply and early, and a pass leaves a small but real business. B's biggest holes (no-reference entrant fails scored RFPs and 100% bonds, thin or negative margin against ISPs at 0.85-0.90x OEM, an unverifiable insurer wrap) are structural and cannot be fixed by the founders alone.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are weak. Each has about a 2-3% unconditional chance of the roughly $110-120M revenue upside, a median of about $30M revenue at break-even, and no moat for years. I picked the one with the better expected outcome for the capital and time it needs.

A is a trading and brokerage business in the middle of a well-documented physical shortage. Its demand side is the strongest evidence in either file, and the downside is bounded by matched-book rules, a 25% cap on unsold units and a $15M early exposure limit. Early cash is available from fee-only brokerage while the company learns whether OEMs will assign slots. If it works, the result is a dealer-financier with $8-12M EBITDA that has several natural acquirers. The risks are real. Dealers already stock and quote units. The supply tiers are unevidenced. The 2028-29 capacity wave may collapse the premium. The model has no moat and the margin is thin.

B is a fixed-price, risk-bearing prime with no hardware and no references, selling to buyers who score references over price. The Austin RFP shows this directly: the winner scored 61, and an unreferenced entrant would top out near 39. Its demand gate and its unit economics pull against each other, because the pass test requires 10% or more cost growth while the margin only works if growth is 9% or less. At the ISP price level, margin is about 3-4% before bond premiums. It also depends on a sponsor, a surety and an insurer wrap that no one has produced evidence for, and it cannot earn before 2028. Even its upside yields only $4-7M EBITDA. A is risky but has the larger and faster payoff, and B's most likely failure points cannot be tested in two weeks.
result.a_biggest_risk: The supply side: nothing shows that an OEM will assign cancelled or in-production units, or accept a newcomer's pooled-deposit reservation. Existing dealers (Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) may already deliver new, warranted units fast enough. If so, the business is a thin-margin broker with a premium that compresses as new OEM capacity arrives in 2028-29.
result.b_biggest_risk: Qualification and unit economics. A no-reference entrant loses scored RFPs and cannot get 100% bonds without a sponsor. Where owners can switch, they already have ISP turnkey offers at 0.85-0.90x OEM price, so the cap is priced at a 3-4% margin. Meanwhile the company holds $20-25M of fixed-price scope-growth risk, with the shops that control rotor slots as its own competitors.

decisive_factors: Median outcomes: A is a modestly profitable, capital-light regional business (about $20M revenue, 0-7% EBITDA, a few million of capital). B's own median burns $28-60M, reaches roughly $17M revenue and breaks even only around year 8-9. B's author says the median is 'not a good business'.

Falsifiability and time cost: A's make-or-break variable (will shops pay $50 or more an hour) can be tested for under $500 in two weeks with real order forms. B's riskiest assumption (owners release the money, 5-6% realized against 20% targeted) takes about 12 months to observe. The 14-day test only measures stated intent from friendly contacts.

Core value proposition: A sells a scarce input (technicians) against a real open requisition that earns the shop $149 an hour. B asks a CFO to pay about 1.1-1.3x a year of savings for capital and authority the CFO already owns. B's own claim is 'parity with DIY', and Redress, in-house teams and renegotiation sit at lower cost.

Capital and structure: A has no funded engineering, receivables are weekly-billed, and customers are small shops that decide fast. B funds $1M or more of engineering per client up front, needs E&O insurance, SOC 2 and a lender, and faces 9-18 month enterprise cycles. Its 36-month annuity and revenue cliff make growth hard to sustain.

Tails are similar and both poor: about 1-2% for A and 2-4% for B to reach $100M. B's tail is slightly fatter, but it sits behind much more capital and a negative-value median, so it does not offset the base case.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and neither has a believable $100M path. The question is which has the better expected outcome net of capital and time.

Idea A is a hire-train-deploy technician staffing business. Its main objection is price. A 93% markup against a 35-45% staffing norm is probably wrong. LAUNCH's postings imply a bill rate of about $34-39. The tenure and conversion math also contradicts itself, and the WIOA subsidy is likely unavailable. Those are serious, and the price objection may well be fatal. But they are cheap and fast to learn: a $500, two-week test of 40 shops with order forms. If the test fails you lose almost nothing. If it passes, you hold a real if low-margin business. It sells into a documented shortage, and the shop earns about $149 an hour on the labor it buys. It needs no vans and no funded engineering. At a median of about $20M revenue it is plausibly profitable with a few million of capital.

Idea B is outcome-priced IT run-cost retirement. It faces several correlated objections at once. Realization was 5-6% against a 20% target. It is unclear why a CFO would pay for execution the CFO already owns. Alternatives are cheaper, such as Redress at 25% once, in-house teams, and renegotiation. The fee equals about 1.1-1.3 years of savings. Insurance, SOC 2 and lender terms are unresolved. The author's own median burns $28M or more, with negative EBITDA until year 8-9. Learning whether it works takes about a year, not two weeks. The upside needs five or six assumptions to hold together.

An early kill limits B's downside. But the conditional-on-success median is still a poor business, so A has the higher expected outcome.
result.a_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a roughly 1.9x markup (about $50 or more an hour against a $27 wage). They hire directly at $24-28, or the market only supports the $34-39 staffing norm. In that case unit economics break near $47.50, and tenure and conversion leakage push EBITDA to about zero even if they do pay.
result.b_biggest_risk: Realization. After a CFO backs the program, business owners do not release enough identified run spend, so invoice lines do not fall and the fee base never exists. The evidence is 5-6% realized against 20% targeted. Compounding this, the CFO has cheaper alternatives (Redress, in-house, renegotiation) and the company funds the engineering, so low realization means heavy cash burn with little revenue.

decisive_factors: A's central risk (will shops pay about $50/hr) can be tested in two weeks for under $500, and revenue pilots can start within months. B's central risks need a winter-long controlled trial (about 20 months) before capitation revenue is even plausible.

A sells a familiar product, hourly staffing plus a training-to-hire conversion, into a documented shortage with a known buyer (the shop owner with an open requisition). B asks a risk-averse landlord to carve out its worst homes and take outcome risk. Two critics rated B's go-to-market and procurement as fatal, no precedent was found, and buyers are bundling and insourcing instead.

The downside floors differ. If A's $52 bill rate fails, it can fall back to a smaller training-and-placement or dealer-academy business with real cash flow. If B's concentration or persistence test fails, or the buyers never appear, the company has nothing to sell, and its fallback of fix-only subcontracting to primes pays prime-level margins.

Capital and geography: A needs little before its 90-day gates and its cost per head is known. B needs about GBP1M before the trial result, then GBP6-10M equity, then a GBP30-60M fund. It also depends on UK procurement law, FSMA perimeter questions and a category that does not yet exist.

The probability-weighted tails are comparable (both critics put $100M at about 1-2% or less), but A's middle outcome of $10-25M of revenue is much more probable than B's median, which only applies after clearing a 30% data gate and a trial.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are long shots at the headline $100M, and both second-round critics put that tail at about 1-2% or lower. So the decision rests on the probability of a decent mid-size outcome, how fast the cheap tests resolve, and what happens if the key assumption fails.

A is a conventional hire-train-deploy labor business. Its main flaw is thin economics: a 93% markup against a 35-45% norm, a break-even bill rate near $47.50, tenure and conversion assumptions that contradict each other, and WIOA subsidy that is probably unavailable. Those are serious, but they are the kind of pricing and retention risks that a two-week outreach to 40 shops and a 90-day pilot will settle. The shortage is real. Temp-to-hire technician staffing already exists, and Tradesmen International shows skilled-trades staffing can pass $100M. If the full markup fails, the business can still run at lower scale as a trained-entrant placement or academy-for-dealers company.

B has a clever core idea and honest self-critique, but it stacks sequential dependencies. The 5-8% of homes must be concentrated and persistent, a landlord must hand over its ledger, and a randomized trial must show a cut of 40% or more through a winter. The trial also collides with Awaab's Law, and the pricing basis was shown to be internally inconsistent. After that, a new outcome-priced contract category has to appear, capital has to be raised, and primes have to subcontract. Procurement turnover tests exclude a newco. Wates and Mears already sell adjacent bundles, and buyers are insourcing. First real revenue is years away, and blended EBITDA is only 8-12% on pass-through works.

A fails faster and cheaper, and it has more ways to land a $10-25M outcome. B's expected value rests on a category that may never form.
result.a_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50/hr (a 93% markup over a $27 wage, with break-even near $47.50). They can hire direct at $24-28, and a comparable temp-technician competitor appears to bill around $34-39 for experienced techs. Conversion that becomes free after about 1,000 hours would also push tenure toward 6 months, which roughly doubles the graduates needed and takes EBITDA to about zero.
result.b_biggest_risk: No landlord buys the product. There is no precedent for a capitated or outcome-priced carve-out of a landlord's worst homes. Buyers are bundling whole-stock deals and insourcing, the incumbents (Wates, Mears) can add a gain-share schedule at no cost, and a newco fails the procurement turnover and D&B tests. Even if the data gate passes, revenue depends on a category that does not yet exist and on a winter-long trial.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk before the fatal objection is tested. A's make-or-break assumption (a shop pays $50 or more an hour) is a $500, two-week test. B's equivalent (small fiscal agents that earn margin and sell near 1.0x revenue) is cheap to test, but if it passes the thesis needs about $25M for the median case and $60-75M for the upside.

Median-case economics. A's median (about $20M revenue, 7% EBITDA, a few million dollars of capital) is a plausible regional business. B's median (about $25M revenue at 5-8% EBITDA on about $25M invested) implies 12-20x EBITDA paid, a probable capital loss, so it is really a bear case.

Sector fundamentals. Medicaid fiscal agents lost 12.5% in aggregate in Wisconsin at competitive prices, face policy and fraud-crackdown risk, and carry tail liability (Section 3504 joint liability, a $162M wage-hour settlement). A's demand is a documented technician shortage, and it has fallback paths (placement fees, employer-funded training) that still earn something.

Competitive structure. B must buy small targets while H.I.G. and General Atlantic pay about 10x for the same kind of asset, and its upside is a joint event of several low-probability conditions. A's refined model sidesteps the PE-funded mobile-PM incumbents and sells open requisitions rather than a share of a fleet's PM wallet.
result.reasons:
Both ideas were wounded in the second critique round, and both $100M cases are unlikely. The earlier critics put A at 1-2% and B at 8-10% or less, and B's own arithmetic makes its upside a joint event. So the decision rests on the median outcome, the capital needed, and how cheaply each can fail.

A is a staffing-plus-training business with a demand signal that is real: roughly 20% of technician slots are unfilled, shop labor bills at $149 an hour, and Level-1 techs earn about $27. The critics' hits are real. The 93% markup is unproven, the conversion economics contradict the tenure assumption, the WIOA subsidy is likely unavailable, and the Michigan supervision rule is a constraint. But the bill-rate question can be answered for under $500, and a pass leads to small pilots, not an acquisition. If $52 an hour fails, there is a credible fallback in placement fees or employer-funded training. The median is a $10-25M regional business at roughly 5-7% EBITDA, and it needs only low single-digit millions in capital.

B is a financial roll-up that needs a seasoned co-founder and a sponsor. Its unit economics are thin: Wisconsin's four fiscal agents lost 12.5% in aggregate. Its margin thesis depends on an unsized premium segment, and its buy price is internally inconsistent: 1.0x revenue is not 6x EBITDA at 5-8% margins. Even if the $103M upside hits, the return is about 1.4-2.1x over seven years. Policy and liability risk are large and cannot be diversified away.

A has a lower ceiling than hoped but a much better risk-adjusted outcome.
result.a_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of $50 or more an hour (about 1.85x the $27 wage, against a 35-45% norm) for six-week-trained Level-1 techs, because they can hire direct at $24-28 and conversion becomes free after about 1,000 hours. That would break the unit economics, since break-even is about $47.50.
result.b_biggest_risk: The acquisition thesis fails on price and margin. Small non-sponsor fiscal agents either do not earn the assumed 15-20% margin at $110 or more per participant per month, or they will only sell at a multiple (above 1.5x revenue) that PE buyers like H.I.G. and General Atlantic already set. The company then pays 12-20x EBITDA for a business that loses money at competitive-bid prices.

decisive_factors: Cost and speed of learning: A's decisive unknown (will shops pay about $50 an hour) is testable for under $500 in two weeks, with first revenue in months. B needs a sponsor, a surety line, insurer indications and two reference awards before first revenue, realistically spring 2028.

Capital at risk and tail shape: A's early losses are small payroll and cohort costs, and a failed pilot costs little. B carries a fixed-price tail, with $20-25M of retained-risk capital needed before event 1 and a bad early loss able to wipe the company.

Fixability of the fatal objections: A's fatal critiques mostly kill the $100M thesis and leave a $10-25M regional business. B's three fatal critiques hit the core mechanism: scored RFPs and bonds a no-reference entrant cannot clear, an insurer wrap that is probably uninsurable, and an incumbent that can copy the clause.

Optionality and adjacent pivots: if Level-1 bench pricing fails, A can still sell experienced-tech temp-to-hire (LAUNCH precedent), placement fees, or employer-paid training, in a documented labor shortage. B's fallback is a crowded, bond-gated plain independent contractor.

Quality of the profit pool: both are thin and mostly pass-through (A 5-12% EBITDA, B about $4-7M EBITDA at $100M revenue). The edge goes to the one a normal capable team can actually staff and execute, since B also needs deep power-industry credibility and a financial sponsor outside the founders' control.
result.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive in absolute terms. Both were wounded by their own refinement, both put the real chance of $100M at 1-3%, and both have mediocre median outcomes. A median is about $20M revenue at 5-7% EBITDA, roughly $1-1.5M. B's median is a subscale break-even company that might sell to an independent service provider (ISP) for $20-40M. So the question is which has the better probability-weighted outcome per dollar and year at risk, and that favors A.

A's weakness is a single, falsifiable assumption: shops will pay about $50 or more an hour for six-week-trained Level-1 technicians. The evidence is not kind. LAUNCH's pay and conversion terms imply a bill rate of roughly $34-39 for experienced techs. The conversion fee and tenure are internally inconsistent, and WIOA on-the-job-training subsidies likely exclude hire-out structures. But the company can learn this in two weeks for under $500 and before any capital is committed. It operates in a real, documented labor shortage with proven analogs (Tradesmen International, LAUNCH). If the Level-1 price point fails, there are adjacent pivots.

B is slow and gated on things the founders do not control. It needs a $15M or larger sponsor, a surety willing to bond a start-up, an insurer view that contradicts the New York no-fortuity opinion, and shop slots in a casting squeeze where ISPs serve their own customers first. Its own pass condition (as-found growth of 10% or more) selects the cases where margin falls to about 3-4%. Hanwha can copy the cap. Buyers scored references over price in the Austin RFP. Its 18 months of overhead before first revenue and its fixed-price tail make a bad outcome expensive, while the upside is only $4-7M EBITDA.

A has the higher chance of becoming a real business, a cheaper way to fail, and more pivots.
result.a_biggest_risk: The core price assumption fails: shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of $50 or more per hour (about 1.9x the Level-1 wage) for six-week-trained technicians when they can hire direct at $24-28. Evidence from LAUNCH implies $34-39 for experienced techs. Below about $47.50 the unit economics break, and rational early conversion of workers to the customer's payroll makes even the median roughly break-even.
result.b_biggest_risk: A no-reference start-up cannot qualify to sell the product: buyers' scoring (50 of 100 points on technical plan and track record) and 100% performance bonds screen it out, while the insurer wrap is probably uninsurable. The company therefore depends on an outside sponsor, a surety and shop slots it does not control, and carries uncapped scope-growth risk on a thin 10-12% margin.

decisive_factors: Demand-side proof: A has a documented, acute shortage and real analogs (Penske's six-week program, LAUNCH TransTechs, Tradesmen at $100M+). B has no US precedent of a health system choosing a non-national operator over cash or a national's offer, and its one documented customer (Kootenai) fired the operator.

Fatal-objection quality: A's pricing assumption ($50+/hr) is untested and could fail, but it can be repriced or restructured. B stacks unresolved structural risks (Medicare 1833(h)(5)(A) wholly-owned rule, EKRA, 42 CFR 424.73, OIG, state laws) on a cost-advantage claim that needs about 20% savings from a startup with no route density.

Sales and capital shape: A sells to many small buyers in weeks and falls back to a $10-25M regional business that consolidators would buy. B needs about 10-15 five-year CFO contracts with slow cycles and a lab-industry insider founder. Its $110M upside needs $70M+ of outside capital and sponsor decisions, and its realistic floor is a $2-6M advisory boutique.

Testability and downside: A's $500 test of 40 shop calls gives a hard price signal in two weeks. B's test needs 20 hospital finance leaders to share cost data and a counsel opinion, and passing it proves little about a 5-year contract.
result.reasons: Both ideas are wounded and both have roughly 1-3% odds of hitting $100M revenue, so the call turns on probability of a good-enough outcome, floor, and capital. A is a thin-margin staffing and training business. Median EBITDA is about 7%, and about 0% if the tenure and conversion contradiction holds. Its enterprise value at scale is modest. Even so, it addresses a real, measured pain (ATRI 65.5% of shops understaffed, 19.3% of slots unfilled). The training model is proven in production at Penske. The buyers are thousands of small shops, so each sale is quick and the idea is cheap to falsify. If $52/hr fails, the same academy can pivot to a lower-bill-rate plus placement-fee or employer-funded model. The floor is a $10-25M regional business, and PE-backed consolidators like Amerit and True North are active buyers of exactly that pipeline. B is a more elegant but more fragile concept. Its viability rests on a legally contested structure, a 20% cost advantage that nobody has benchmarked, and a startup winning 5-year contracts against Quest, Labcorp, Orion, TriCore and Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice. Its value-if-it-works is similar to A's, but it comes through three stacked layers needing sponsor capital. The one operator precedent (PAML) ended in acquisition by a competitor, and Kootenai insourced after leaving the model. The expected outcome favors A.
result.a_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a roughly 93% markup (about $50-52/hr against a $27 wage; break-even about $47.50) for 6-week Level-1 trainees when they can hire direct at $24-28. Free conversion after about 1,000 hours also shortens tenure, and WIOA subsidies likely exclude hire-out staffing. Together these push margins to about zero.
result.b_biggest_risk: No non-selling health system has been shown to sign a 5-year open-book operating contract with a startup at a price at least 8% below its own cost, rather than insourcing, buying advice from Mayo/ARUP/Chi, or taking a national's management deal. That demand-plus-cost-advantage claim is unbenchmarked and has no precedent, and the structure is also exposed to Medicare 1833(h)(5)(A) and EKRA.

decisive_factors: Capital and time to find out: A's key assumption (a shop pays at least $50/hr for pre-trained Level-1s) can be falsified for under $500 in two weeks, and a failed pilot costs little. B needs a $100-175M equity partner plus a proven casting operator, and about a 35% chance of closing even a first deal.

Fatality of the objections: A's two fatal critiques are scoped to the $100M thesis, and a $10-25M regional business survives them. B's three fatal critiques hit its existence: no precedent for OEM prepay to a non-incumbent, a sources-and-uses gap, and a customer value proposition near nil, since the customer could sign the same deal with the plant's current owner.

Return quality if it works: B's own upside gives about 1.8-3.3x gross and low-to-mid-teens IRR, which may not raise the equity at all. result.reasons:
I would back A, but only narrowly, because neither idea is attractive on expected value.

A, in its refined form, is a thin dealer-financier. Gross margin is realistically 7-10%, the median case is roughly break-even at about $30M of revenue, and the $120M upside is about 2-3% likely and partly overstated. The competition critique is largely correct: Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr and FluxCo already work this space, and the supply of cancelled or assignable OEM slots is unevidenced. Still, the market is real. Lead times run 128-160 weeks, buyers do pay for speed, and intermediaries have reached $100M or more of orders on tens of millions of capital. The decisive point is that A's biggest risk can be tested in two weeks for almost nothing. It can start earning brokerage fees without inventory, and it can scale its capital at risk in steps after that.

B is more likely to be fatal. Its keystone is an OEM prepayment with make-whole to a non-incumbent owner, and nobody found a precedent for it. The money Doncasters, Howmet and Chromalloy already get shows customers pay incumbents, not a new sponsor. The target-acquisition prices rest on a non-comparable deal, and qualified assets trade at 6-8x revenue. B needs $130-175M of equity and a proven operator, and its own numbers give mid-teens returns. The founder ends up as originator with a small stake, and the unconditional median is $0. Even if everything lines up, B mostly earns a capital return, not an operating edge. A's cheap, fast, mostly reversible path wins on risk-adjusted outcome, though only by a small margin.
result.a_biggest_risk: The speed premium and slot supply are unproven. Existing dealers and intermediaries (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr, FluxCo) may already deliver warranted units fast enough, and no source shows OEMs will let a newcomer assign cancelled or reserved slots. That would leave only a roughly 5-8% spread boutique with no moat.
result.b_biggest_risk: The capital stack never closes. No OEM has been shown to prepay with make-whole to a non-incumbent owner, and the same customer money goes to Doncasters or Howmet instead. Qualified casters are also priced far above the assumed 2x revenue and are being bought by better-capitalized bidders (GE, Arcline, Pursuit, Doncasters).

decisive_factors: A's core unit economics are contradicted by its own materials: a 93% staffing markup against a 35-45% norm, free conversion after ~1,000 hours that rational shops will use at 6-12 months, and training cost that cannot be amortized over that tenure. The critic's recomputation puts median EBITDA at about -5% to 0% instead of +7%.

A's demand evidence is misapplied, since the shortage is of qualified technicians, not Level-1 slots. Penske, Love's and Ryder insource the same 6-week model, shops can hire a $16-28 entry tech directly, and no evidence was found that anyone buys temporary trainee technicians at scale. WIOA subsidy is likely ineligible for hired-out staffing.

B's market is validated by real transactions: HomeServe Deutschland, Konzmann, Builtech and VINCI show Handwerk roll-ups reaching EUR 100M+ of revenue. Seller supply is structurally abundant (about 54,000 planned closures against 49,000 handovers, with a record 4,950 insolvencies).

B's deal design limits downside. Books are bought at 0.25-0.40x of retained revenue with 40-50% contingent, and the targets are real customers, crews and vans. The failure modes (sellers refuse, books are consumer-heavy) are caught by a two-week ledger test and a month-12 gate, and the fallback is a small, self-funded regional group.

A and B have similar median size ($20M vs $27.6M revenue) and similar thin median profit, and both reach $100M with only about 1-3% probability. So the call turns on which has the higher chance of working at all. A's likely-fatal flaw is arithmetic and market-structure. B's flaws, capital and the invented 19% contribution, mostly cap the upside rather than kill the median.
result.reasons:
Both ideas ended wounded, with a credible $100M probability of only about 1-3% and thin median profit (A about $1.5M EBITDA at best, B about EUR 0.8M group EBIT). So the decision turns on which is more likely to work at all, and which objections are more likely fatal.

A's central objections look structural. The business sells a 6-week-trained Level-1 technician at a 93% markup. Its own materials show the break-even bill rate is about $47.50, and LAUNCH's experienced-tech postings imply a bill of only $34-39. The pricing makes conversion free after about 1,000 hours, so rational customers convert early, tenure drops to about 6 months, and training cost per FTE-year roughly triples. The second-round critic's arithmetic puts median EBITDA at about -5% to 0%. The demand figures measure a shortage of qualified techs, not Level-1 slots. The biggest employers (Penske, Love's, Ryder) insource this exact model. WIOA subsidies are likely off the table for hired-out labor. It is also a 1,000-head W-2 staffing business with workers' comp and negligent-training exposure. It is cheap to test, but I think it is more likely to fail the test than pass it.

B's objections are serious but mostly cap the upside. The buy-side market is proven by actual deals, and seller supply is abundant and growing. Contingent pricing and acquiring real customers, crews and vans give structural downside protection. The model ties to standard roll-up route-density logic, and the failure modes are caught early by a ledger-based test, so a small self-funded regional group is a plausible floor. Its flaws are real: no identified anchor LP, an invented 19% contribution figure, adverse selection among sellers, Meister and HWK constraints, and crowded competition. These mostly constrain scale rather than kill the median case.

B is slightly more likely to produce some real business, so I pick B, though it is a close call.
result.a_biggest_risk: Shops and dealers will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of about $50 an hour (a 93% markup) for 6-week-trained Level-1 technicians when they can hire direct at $24-28. Even at that rate, free conversion after about 1,000 hours erodes tenure, so training costs are never recovered and EBITDA falls to about zero or below.
result.b_biggest_risk: Not enough owner-led Elektro/SHK firms have retainable B2B service books and will accept the contingent 0.25-0.40x formula, because adverse selection leaves the owner-dependent, consumer-heavy books. The invented 19% contribution and 70% retention then fail, and no anchor LP funds the EUR 10M+ follow-on tranche, so the business stays at roughly breakeven scale.

decisive_factors: Objection severity: B drew two 'fatal' critiques (no evidence anyone buys a capitated carve-out; a newco cannot clear procurement, turnover or D&B tests). B's own dossier says 'weak, leaning kill'. A's critiques were all 'serious' and its dossier says 'not dead'.

Demand evidence: A sells into an existing category (contingency, savings-share and decommissioning services such as Redress, SoftwareOne, PRGX and ProsperOps), to US CFOs with their own budgets. B has no carve-out precedent, and buyers are bundling and insourcing.

Entry and fallback: A starts with a paid $75-150k X-ray, so cash arrives in months 2-4, and it has a smaller capital-light fallback. B's first step is a free x-ray, its capitated rung needs GBP20-40M of risk capital, and its fallback is a commodity fix-only contractor against Wates and Mears.

Testability and market: A's riskiest assumption (owner follow-through) can be tested with exports from 3 companies in 14 days, and its US market is larger. B is a single-country market with slow procurement, FSMA and Awaab's Law complications, and a key causal result that needs a full winter (about 20 months).
result.reasons:
Neither idea is attractive. Both median cases are about $17M of thin-margin services revenue, and both $100M upsides sit near 2-4% by the authors' own numbers. The question is which one is more likely to die early.

B has the more dangerous objections. Two of its three critics called it fatal, and the objections are about buyer behaviour and the procurement door, not about tuning the model. Landlords are bundling whole-stock deals and insourcing. Winchester and Livin set turnover and D&B tests that a newco cannot pass. Wates already sells Healthy Homes. The signer's gain is under 0.5% of turnover while the landlord keeps the statutory duty. No capitated carve-out precedent exists. result.a_biggest_risk: Business owners do not release the identified retirable spend, so realization stays near 25-30% (5-6% was seen against a 20% target). The fee base then barely exists, and the CFO's cheaper alternatives (Redress, in-house, renegotiation) are at parity with this offer.

decisive_factors: A has no structural legal blocker; B has to clear several regulatory hurdles at once (Medicare referral-lab billing, the billing-agent pay rule, EKRA, OIG, state transaction laws). Each one can kill it or make it heavier than its margin supports.

B's median is about $7-8M revenue, its stated odds of signing a second client are about 55%, and its $110M upside is mostly pass-through revenue at roughly 8% EBITDA.

result.reasons:

A is a thin-margin services business at median, with about $17M revenue and break-even around year 8-9 if it funds engineering heavily. It has no statute or regulator standing between it and revenue. The evidence is 20% targeted and 5-6% realized. A related risk is that CFOs cap the share near 15-20% or choose Redress or an in-house program instead.
result.b_biggest_risk: Demand and price: a non-selling health system won't sign a 5-year open-book contract with an unproven startup at a price at least 8% below its own cost, rather than taking a national's offer, a regional operator, or doing it in-house. The cost advantage is unbenchmarked, and the structure also has to clear the Medicare referral-lab, billing-agent pay and EKRA rules.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk is staged for A. The first gates are a 14-day test, paid X-rays by day 60 and a signed agreement by day 120, and they cost founder time rather than tens of millions. B has to put real acquisition capital to work, and its own refined pitch puts the full plan at $60-75M.

A's upside is a real business, with 20-50% contribution margins and $20-44M of EBITDA at $100M revenue. B's upside is $100M of revenue at 5-8% margin, which the critic calculates returns only 1.4-2.1x on capital over about 7 years. A 9% chance of a roughly break-even payoff is worth less than A's 2-4% chance of a large payoff.

The sector faces a federal fraud push, state cuts to self-direction, joint-and-several payroll-tax liability and a $162M Calderon-type wage-hour tail. The why-now is mostly spent. A faces a go-to-market problem, but its underlying economics (pay a share of a verified invoice drop) are sound.
result.reasons:
Both ideas were wounded in the second round and neither is attractive, so this is a close call between two weak options. I weighed expected value against capital and time.

B is a roll-up of small Medicaid fiscal agents. It needs $60-75M of sponsor-style capital to buy operators in a sector where the only public cost data shows a combined -12.5% margin. The pitch's own median case earns $1.3-2M of EBITDA on about $25M invested. The critic's arithmetic puts that at 12-20x paid, so the median is a capital loss. Even the 8-10% upside returns about 1.4-2.1x over roughly 7 years. Its odds of $100M are an honest 2-4%. But it deploys money only after gates (paid X-rays, a signed program agreement, an E&O quote, first audited invoice drops), with an explicit instruction to stop rather than shrink. If it works at the upside, it is a 20-40% EBITDA business, and the unit economics improve as AI makes retirement engineering cheaper.

A's most likely fatal flaw is "why would a CFO pay 26-30% for something he could do himself or buy from Redress at 25% once." Realization is also a large risk, at 5-6% realized against 20% targeted in the evidence. But A fails cheaply and early. B can fail after the capital is spent.

Even if they do, the CFO can get most of the value through DIY, renegotiation or Redress at 25% invoiced once. In that case the fee base is zero, or the company is an undifferentiated $5M advisory boutique.

Small fiscal agents with healthy margins probably do not exist at a price the cash flow can carry, because sellers anchor on the 10x sponsor deals and the only sellable books are the money-losing ones. The thesis then needs $60-75M of capital to earn thin margins, with Medicaid policy and 3504/wage-hour liability tails stacked on top. The median is a capital loss and even the upside returns about 1.4-2.1x.

decisive_factors: Value per revenue dollar: A's upside path reaches $20-45M EBITDA at $100-120M revenue, while B's $110M upside yields only $4-7M EBITDA because revenue is mostly pass-through parts. At similar low odds (2-4% vs 3%), A's tail is worth several times more.

Both medians are poor (A about $17M revenue at break-even in year 8-9; B about $30M and a small sale to an ISP). That does not separate them, so the upside quality and speed of invalidation decide it.
result.reasons:

result.a_biggest_risk: Realization. Business owners do not release the identified retirable spend (the evidence is about 5-6% realized against 20% targeted), so third-party invoice lines never fall. The company would then have funded engineering with no fee base. CFOs capping the share at 20% or less, or choosing Redress or in-house work at roughly DIY parity, would make that worse.

That leaves a margin of about 3-5% while the prime retains scope-growth and schedule risk. It has no moat against Hanwha, and it depends on a sponsor, a surety and shop slots it cannot control.

decisive_factors: A's downside is bounded and cheap to learn. A 14-day test, then paid X-rays by day 60, with hard kill gates, means the team finds out within about 12 months at low cost. B's decisive proof (an OEM prepaying a non-incumbent) has never been observed, and B needs $130-175M of other people's equity plus a proven casting operator before it is real.

B's objections are structurally fatal, A's are mostly about size and price. All three critics called B fatal and the dossier calls it dead as a founder-led startup. The customer-side value proposition is close to nil, since OEM money can go straight to the incumbent (Doncasters, Howmet, Chromalloy). The edge over Pursuit, Arcline and CPP in buying scarce assets is thin. Even the upside returns only about 1.8-3.3x gross.

A's market is broad and the demand precedent is real. About 700 reachable payers, against 20-25 for B. Savings-share and recovery-audit models exist (PRGX, Redress, ProsperOps), and a paid entry product gives cash in months 2-4. B's unconditional median is $0.
